newsitem.title: SPAIN: Past, present Spain leaders mark 20-year democracy.
newsitem.headline: Past, present Spain leaders mark 20-year democracy.

text.p: The four past and present prime ministers of Spain's young democracy gathered together on Friday to mark the 20th anniversary of the first general election after nearly 40 years of dictatorship.

Adolfo Suarez, who was elected amid joyous street celebrations on June 15, 1977, led the country through its first trembling steps back to democracy after the fascist dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.
He was joined for the anniversary at Moncloa, the prime minister's residence in Madrid, by Leopoldo Calvo Sotelo, Felipe Gonzalez and current Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
Wearing sombre suits but appearing relaxed and jovial, the four men posed for photographs before going inside to discuss their roles in Spain's democratic transformation.
"The first legislative elections were the culmination of the process of democratisation in Spain," government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told a news conference.
"Twenty years later, Spaniards can feel satisfied because advances in the liberties and democratic values gained in this period have been the fruit of efforts by society as a whole."
Calvo Sotelo, who took over when Suarez resigned in 1981 and ruled until Gonzalez won a 1982 election, said he remembered the transition as a step-by-step learning process.
"There were a lot of mistakes and a lot of problems, but we did what we did well," he told journalists.

Many of the deputies elected on June 15, 1977, had spent years in exile and had no experience in government. Political parties were immature and campaigning was often haphazard, but people felt it was one of Spain's greatest moments.

There was enormous turnout for the election, in which most people were voting for the first time. The last democratic election had been in 1936, a few months before Franco took over at the start of the three-year Spanish Civil War.

"It was one of the best, purest and most emotional days that a Spanish citizen could have the fortune to participate in," said Gabriel Cisneros, elected as a member of Suarez's now-defunct Union of the Democratic Centre (UCD) party.
"Everyone, voters and deputies, knew the joy that we were starting something new for this country regardless of their party affiliation or who they were voting for."
Suarez's party won the election, with Gonzalez's Socialist Workers Party emerging as the main opposition and the recently- legalised Communist Party of Spain as the third biggest party.

The election ushered in years of heady change in Spain, which had been isolated and stuck in the past under the long dictatorship. The country's institutions all needed reform to erase the totalitarian practices that had permeated daily life.
"We had to work fast. We were in a hurry," said Jordi Sole Tura, a Socialist member of the first parliament and one of the creators of Spain's constitutiion.

"We had to build a democracy, and at the same time confront the unresolved problems of the past like building a welfare system, a pension system, health care for everyone, education for everyone. We had to join Europe."
